At its most direct, ordure means excrement — the solid waste that passes out of the body of a human or an animal after digestion. Put simply, it is a formal word for feces, dung, or filth of that kind.

If you walked into a barn and the floor was covered in animal waste, you could accurately say the barn was covered in ordure. If a medieval street had human and animal waste running through it (which was common), a writer of the time might describe the stench of ordure filling the air.

So ordure = excrement, dung, feces.
Why Does Such a Word Even Exist?

English has many words for the same basic thing — feces, dung, excrement, waste, manure, filth. The reason ordure exists alongside all of them is one of tone and register.

Ordure is a formal, literary, and somewhat elevated word. You would not use it in casual conversation. You would find it in:

  • Old or classic literature
  • Formal or scholarly writing
  • Historical texts
  • Poetic or stylistic writing where the author wants to sound deliberate and precise

Think of it this way: a farmer would say dung. A child might say poop. A scientist might say feces. But a Victorian novelist or a serious essayist might write ordure — not to be fancy for no reason, but because the word carries a weight and gravity that suits serious prose.

Beyond its literal meaning, ordure is very commonly used figuratively — meaning it is used to describe something that is morally disgusting, utterly vile, deeply offensive, or corrupt, in the same way that excrement is physically revolting.

When a critic says a piece of writing is ordure, they are not saying it is literally made of feces. They are saying it is as disgusting and worthless as filth — that it is morally repugnant, degrading, obscene, or simply garbage of the worst kind.

This figurative use is powerful precisely because of the literal meaning behind it. Calling something ordure is a cutting, contemptuous insult. It says: "This thing is not just bad — it is as low and repulsive as human waste."

Examples of things that might be called ordure in this figurative sense:

  • Deeply obscene or degrading speech
  • Morally corrupt propaganda
  • Writing that is considered disgusting or without any redeeming value
  • Any content someone views as utterly vile and beneath contempt
Two Meanings, One Word — A Clear Summary

LiteralPhysical excrement; feces; dung; bodily waste
FigurativeAnything morally disgusting, obscene, vile, or utterly without worth
How It Is Typically Used in a Sentence

Here are example sentences that show the word in action:

Literal use:

  • "The soldiers trudged through the mud and ordure of the battlefield."
  • "The streets of the old city ran with ordure and rainwater."

Figurative use:

  • "The editor refused to publish such ordure and sent the manuscript back immediately."
  • "He dismissed the politician's speech as nothing more than ordure dressed up in fine language."
  • "The pamphlet was full of the most vile ordure — lies, slander, and filth."

Notice how in the figurative examples, the word lands with real force. It is not a mild criticism. It is a complete rejection — a declaration that the thing in question is repulsive and worthless.

1. It is always negative.
Ordure is never used approvingly or neutrally. Whether literal or figurative, it always describes something unpleasant, disgusting, or undesirable.

2. It is a strong word.
Figuratively, calling something ordure is one of the sharpest things you can say. It places the thing in the lowest possible category — not just bad, but filthy.

3. It is not everyday vocabulary.
If you use this word in a text message or casual chat, it will sound odd. It belongs in writing, formal speech, or literary contexts. That said, understanding it is essential for reading classic literature, formal essays, or any older English text.

4. It can refer to a mass or a quality.
You can talk about "a pile of ordure" (a physical mass of waste) or "the ordure of his argument" (the general filthiness or moral repugnance of something). It works both ways.
The One-Sentence Definition You Can Always Return To

Ordure is a formal word meaning excrement or dung in the literal sense, and anything morally vile, obscene, or utterly disgusting in the figurative sense — always used to describe something at the very bottom of what is acceptable or decent.
